title: The kitchen door stays open
hookLine: langar is free to anyone of any background, in many gurdwaras all day

cards: It's two in the afternoon on a Tuesday. You're a college student far from home, down to your last few dollars. Or a truck driver who's been on the road since four.
Or someone who just lost a job and hasn't told anyone yet. You walk past a gurdwara, and someone at the door waves you in. You don't know a word of Punjabi.
You don't know what a Sikh believes. You're not sure you're allowed. You cover your head with a borrowed scarf, take off your shoes, sit down in the row, and a stranger puts hot food in your hands.
Nobody asks your name. Nobody asks why you're hungry.

teach.b: Langar is free, and it's for anyone: any faith or none, any background, any reason for being hungry, or no reason at all. That's not a side rule. It's the whole point.
In many gurdwaras the kitchen runs all day, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar it feeds tens of thousands of people every single day, around the clock.
Remember its four doors from day sixty, facing every direction so anyone from anywhere could walk in? The kitchen has the same shape. No ticket, no sermon to sit through first, no form to fill in.
You do cover your head and take off your shoes, as everyone does. That's respect, not a test. Guru Nanak gives a picture in the Japji that fits the langar hall.
In paraphrase: let wisdom be your food, and compassion the one who hands it out. And Sikhs have taken the open door far beyond the gurdwara.

After floods and earthquakes, at borders, on highways where travelers are stranded, Sikh volunteers set up kitchens and start serving, often before anyone official arrives. The food is simple. The rule is the same.

teach.h: NOTICE WHO ISN'T IN THE ROOM.
teach.b: The open door asks something of the people inside, too: not just to cook, but to keep noticing who isn't in the room yet. The student. The driver.
The person who's embarrassed to come.
The door isn't really open if nobody ever walks out of it to wave someone in.

how: Langar is served free in every gurdwara to anyone who comes, and in many it runs all day; visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes, and Sikh volunteers also run langar kitchens at disasters and for travelers in need.

o: the Guru's free kitchen, open to anyone
a meal served only to baptized Sikhs
a feast held on the Gurus' birthdays

games.q: what's inside the open door — tap the pairs.
p: the one who hands out the food

s: you must be a Sikh to eat langar
it's for anyone, of any faith or none, no questions asked.
the Harmandir Sahib's langar feeds tens of thousands every day
the kitchen runs around the clock.
visitors must listen to a sermon before they eat
there's no ticket, no sermon and no form. you cover your head and take off your shoes, as everyone does.

games.q: you're serving in a langar hall. a stranger hovers at the door, clearly unsure whether they're allowed in. what does the open door ask of you?
o: wait to see if they come in on their own.
ask them a few questions first.
walk out, wave them in, and find them a scarf.
games.why: the door isn't really open if nobody walks out of it to wave someone in. langar asks no questions.

practice: Picture the places you move through in a normal week: your street, your work or school, the store, the bus.

In your mind, look for the people who might be hungry, or lonely at mealtimes, the new coworker who eats alone, the neighbor who lives by himself, the person you pass on the corner every day, and let each face come and stay a moment.
Don't plan anything big yet; just notice them.

wordCard.voice: Langar. The Guru's kitchen, free to anyone, of any faith or none, no questions asked, in many places all day.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the Guru's kitchen, open to all.

carryVoice: Your line: the door stays open. Any faith or none, nobody asks why. Day one hundred fifteen.
